Q: how to program esp32 after assembly on a PCB A:

Great question for anyone new to PCB assembly with microcontrollers. Once your ESP32 is soldered onto the board, you have a few options depending on how your PCB was designed:

1. USB-to-Serial via onboard bridge (most common) If your PCB includes a USB-to-UART bridge chip (e.g. CP2102, CH340, or FTDI), you can program the ESP32 directly via USB — same as a dev board. Just make sure GPIO0 is pulled LOW during boot to enter flash mode, and EN (reset) is accessible.

2. Exposed programming header If your board has a 4-pin or 6-pin header breaking out TX, RX, GND, 3.3V, GPIO0, and EN, you can connect an external USB-to-serial adapter and flash using esptool or Arduino IDE.

3. JTAG interface For more advanced debugging and programming, expose the JTAG pins (TDI, TDO, TCK, TMS) and use a JTAG debugger. This is useful for production environments.

Best practice for production PCBs: When working with a PCB assembly manufacturer, always ask them to expose a programming header or test points for TX/RX/GPIO0/EN before mass production. This allows in-circuit programming (ICP) directly on the assembled board without desoldering anything.

We do this routinely at our facility — during PCBA we can also handle pre-flash programming of ESP32 modules before shipment if needed. More info at https://tjhxpcb.com/pcb-assembly/

Q: Usage of non-initialized class field 'myMap' when called from function 'main' A:

The IDE's warning is a false positive because new MyClass() will result in value initialization which here will use the default ctor that already correctly initializes the data member myMap using the member initializer list.

In the second case also, where you use const MyClass my_class{};, we have list initialization which in this case will also use the default ctor and thus here also the myMap data member is initialized.

Q: Why am I getting conflicting error messages relating to my strings? A:

The only way that this code:

wc.lpszClassName = g_szClassName;

Can produce different errors is if you are compiling it in different contexts with different compiler configurations.

Most Win32 API structs and functions that deal with strings are declared to use TCHAR strings, which map to either wchar_t or char, and their symbol names have W or A appended to their names, depending on whether or not UNICODE is defined during the precompile stage.

This is explained in more detail on MSDN:

Get Started with Win32 and C++ > Working with Strings

As such...

When the variable is a char variable, it gives the following error:

a value of type "const char *" cannot be assigned to an entity of type "LPCWSTR" (aka "const WCHAR *")

This happens only when you compile the translation unit (.cpp file) with UNICODE defined, where WNDCLASSEX will map to WNDCLASSEXW, which uses wchar_t strings.

When the variable is a wchar_t, I get the following error instead:

'=': cannot convert from 'const wchar_t [14]' to 'LPCSTR'

This happens only when you compile the translation unit without UNICODE defined, so WNDCLASSEX will map to WNDCLASSEXA, which uses char strings.

The same issue applies to other APIs used in your code, including DefWindowProc, RegisterClassEx, CreateWindowEx, MessageBox, etc.

The moral of the story - don't mix your precompiler configurations. Pick one and stick with it. Or else don't rely on TCHAR-based APIs at all, use A and W APIs explicitly as needed.

Q: OS dev and where the boot sector is in qemu A:

It appears that you have hexdumped the file created by the QEMU dump-guest-memory monitor command. This file is not a flat image of the guest machine's memory; rather, it is an ELF core file. As such, the byte locations in the file (shown in the first column of your hexdump) do not correspond directly with the address in the guest's physical memory.

If you have GNU binutils installed, with the elf64-little format supported, you can get a properly labeled hexdump with objdump --full-contents foo.dump. (LLVM's objdump does not seem to handle these core files correctly.) For me, this shows the boot sector contents at the expected address 0x7c00:

 07c00 b40ebb0f 0081c300 7c8a07cd 10ebfe58  ........|......X
 07c10 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000  ................

You can also dump the ELF headers with objdump -h foo.dump. On mine, I get:


foo.dump:     file format elf64-little

Sections:
Idx Name          Size      VMA               LMA               File off  Algn
  0 note0         00000270  0000000000000000  0000000000000000  000001d8  2**0
                  CONTENTS, READONLY
  1 load1         000a0000  0000000000000000  0000000000000000  00000448  2**0
                  CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY
  2 load2         07f40000  00000000000c0000  00000000000c0000  000a0448  2**0
                  CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY
  3 load3         01000000  00000000fd000000  00000000fd000000  07fe0448  2**0
                  CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY
  4 load4         00040000  00000000fffc0000  00000000fffc0000  08fe0448  2**0
                  CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY

This gives the mapping between addresses in the guest's memory and the corresponding regions in the file. The load1 section shows a region of size 0xa0000, starting at guest address 0 and located at offset 0x448 in the file. So the low megabyte in memory appears in the file at a location that is 0x448 more than its address. Indeed, if I hexdump the file, I find the boot sector contents starting at byte 0x8048 in the file, which does equal 0x448 + 0x7c00.

I suspect that if you were to do the same for your file, you would find that the corresponding File off is 0x3c8, the difference between 0x7c00 and the location 0x7fc8 where you found the boot sector code.

Q: Singleton vs Static FUNCTIONS A:

Singletons shouldn't be used just as namespaces or scopes. They should correspond to something, maybe in the real world, that does exist but only once, e.g. a configuration read from a file. In your circumstance that appears to mean that you should use static methods.

Q: correlation analysis between features and target variables in survival analysis A:

In this case, I think you should go with Univariate Cox Proportional Hazards Model or C-index, or you can even go with Random Survival Forest Feature(which is very useful for benchmark studies).
Problem is that in survival analysis the situation is more complex than the standard ML, because the target is not single variable.
Correlation Heatmaps are not ideal for survival data because correlation assumes no censoring but survival dataset contains censored observations. So this heatmap can be misleading
